title: Borscht
subtitle: Eastern European beetroot soup with soured cream
excerpt: A vibrant, deeply coloured Eastern European soup built on slow-cooked beetroot, cabbage, and beef stock. Served with a generous spoonful of soured cream and a scattering of dill.

recipe.sourceNotes: Borscht is one of the defining dishes of Ukrainian, Russian, Polish, and Ashkenazi Jewish cooking, and each culture has its own version. The name comes from the Slavic word for hogweed, an earlier ingredient that was replaced by beetroot as it spread from cultivation. It is eaten across Eastern Europe and the Jewish diaspora, from Ukraine and Poland to Israel and New York. The simplest versions are vegetarian and the most elaborate include beef, short ribs, or beef marrow bones cooked for hours. The beetroot provides the characteristic deep crimson colour and the earthy sweetness; a splash of vinegar at the end sharpens the flavour and heightens the colour. Soured cream (or smetana) and fresh dill are the canonical garnishes.

content.text: Wear gloves when handling raw beetroot: the juice stains skin and clothes permanently. Grate the beetroot on the coarse side of a box grater or use a food processor. Adding a splash of red wine vinegar just before serving preserves and deepens the colour; without it, the soup will dull to a brownish red on standing.

items.preparation: finely shredded; or use savoy cabbage

content.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Fry the onion and carrot for 8 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add the grated beetroot and tinned tomatoes. Cook for 5 minutes.
Add the stock, potatoes, bay leaves, salt, and pepper. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes. Add the shredded cabbage and cook for a further 15 minutes until everything is tender.
Remove the bay leaves. Stir in the red wine vinegar. Taste for seasoning. Ladle into bowls. Add a spoonful of soured cream and a scattering of fresh dill. Serve with dark rye bread.
